newsitem.title: NORWAY: Perry says NATO enlargement on for next year.
newsitem.headline: Perry says NATO enlargement on for next year.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of Defence William Perry, shrugging off Russia's virulent opposition, said on Thursday that NATO's expansion to take in former communist enemies would go ahead next year.
"At a summit next year several countries will be invited to start accession talks," he told reporters after a two-day informal meeting of the alliance's 16 defence ministers.
Perry declined to be drawn on which countries may be invited to join the alliance, but emphasised the process would go ahead despite Russian objections which he maintained were unfounded.
"If I thought that those actions (expansion) were threatening Russia I would have a very different view, but I don't believe that for a minute," Perry said.

Since the end of the Cold War, ex-Communist countries have been seeking to join NATO to guarantee their future security against Russia. Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are the most likely candidates, but could be joined by Slovenia.
NATO hopes to buy off Russia by offering it a new all- embracing security pact which it says it will negotiate in parallel with its first enlargement since the late 1970s.

Perry said he would bring up that issue in talks later on Thursday with his Russian counterpart Igor Rodionov which he said would also centre on how to build on Russia's landmark cooperation in the alliance-led peace mission in Bosnia.

NATO is also hoping it can entice Russia to take part actively in the alliance's Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme designed to try and fill a security vacuum in central and eastern Europe created by the collapse of communism.
The alliance wants to upgrade PFP and offer it as an alternative to countries left out of next year's expansion, but which still want an insurance policy against a rebirth of an expansionist Russia.

"What we are doing with NATO and what we are doing with Partnership for Peace is creating a security circle for all of Europe... our goal is not to threaten Russia, but to bring Russia into that security circle," Perry said.

NATO diplomats say the aim is to try to dovetail approval of both enlargement and a new pact for Russia at next year's heads of government summit which would also endorse reform of the alliance's command structures.
But if that was not possible, Perry made clear that enlargement would go ahead anyway.
"There is a very important principle here, we are open to new nations that are qualified and want to join. We believe that is a very important principle," Perry said.

Germany's Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said there was a consensus on the need to move ahead with expansion, but said it could be done without alienating Moscow. "The time is ripe for a decision to be made at next year's summit," he told reporters, but he said that left plenty of time to reach a "new strategic partnership between a new NATO and a new Russia."

Alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana earlier said the two-day meeting had also made considerable progress towards establishing a "leaner, more efficient NATO" capable of undertaking Bosnia-style crisis-management tasks.
France has indicated it will play a full part in any new NATO.
Perry, citing Washington's naval and air commitment in the Mediterranean, ruled out handing the command post in southern Europe for rotation by European allies as requested by Paris.

Solana said the alliance would also discuss in detail with Rodionov, Russia's participation in any follow-on force the alliance may send to Bosnia next year to continue policing the Dayton peace accords.

Russia has already indicated it would be prepared to serve in that force, but the alliance is set to offer Moscow permanent liaison officers at several command levels to build on contacts created last year in organising the current force.
